title: Nilpotent rigidity of trivial homomorphisms from split diagonalizable groups
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative ring, let $J\subseteq A$ be an ideal with $J^N=0$ for some integer $N\geq1$, and put $S=\operatorname{Spec}A$ and $S_0=\operatorname{Spec}(A/J)$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Let $M$ be a finitely generated additive abelian group. Let $A[M]$ be the free $A$-module with basis $(e_m)_{m\in M}$, with multiplication $e_me_n=e_{m+n}$, unit $e_0$, comultiplication $e_m\mapsto e_m\otimes e_m$, counit $e_m\mapsto1$, and antipode $e_m\mapsto e_{-m}$, and set $H=D_A(M)=\operatorname{Spec}A[M]$ with the resulting group operations. An $S$-group scheme is an $S$-scheme [def-pc-scheme] with multiplication, identity section and inverse satisfying the associativity, unit and inverse diagrams. Let $G$ be any $S$-group scheme and let $f:H\to G$ be an $S$-group homomorphism. Write $e_G:S\to G$ for its identity section and $p:H\to S$ for the structure map. If the base change $f_0:H\times_SS_0\to G\times_SS_0$ [def-pc-base-change] equals the identity-valued homomorphism $e_{G_0}\circ p_0$, then $f=e_G\circ p$. No smoothness, flatness, separatedness or finite-presentation assumption on $G$ is imposed.

source.place: Conrad, Reductive group schemes, Corollary B.2.7, printed p.287 (PDF page index 286), split diagonalizable special case. Read online 2026-10-24; local archive WANTED as literature/conrad-reductive-group-schemes.pdf. No Stacks tag states this rigidity assertion.

proof.text: We first prove the assertion when $J^2=0$, writing $I=J$, $A_0=A/I$, $B=A[M]$ and $B_0=A_0[M]$. Reduction of a finite sum is coefficientwise, so $\ker(B\to B_0)=I[M]=\bigoplus_{m\in M}I e_m$, an ideal of square zero. This is a first order thickening $H_0\hookrightarrow H$. The same holds for $C=A[M\times M]$ and $C_0=A_0[M\times M]$. The tensor-product universal property identifies $B\otimes_A B$ with $C$: the two inverse maps send $e_u\otimes e_v$ to $e_{(u,v)}$ and back. Consequently multiplication $H\times_SH\to H$ corresponds to $\Delta(e_m)=e_{(m,m)}$, and the two projections to $L(e_m)=e_{(m,0)}$, $R(e_m)=e_{(0,m)}$.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-space-square-zero-lift-linearization] with $X=G$, regarded as an algebraic space over $S$, the affine first order thickening $H_0\hookrightarrow H$ over $S$ of step 1 with ideal $\widetilde{I[M]}$, and $a=e_Gp$. Since $f_0=e_Gp|_{H_0}$, $f$ lies in $L_G(e_0)$ with $e_0=e_Gp|_{H_0}$, which is exactly the kernel $K_B$ of $G(B)\to G(B_0)$. The lemma gives a bijection $\theta:K_B\to\operatorname{Hom}(e_0^*\Omega^1_{G/S},\widetilde{I[M]})$, $\theta(b)=b^\sharp-(e_Gp)^\sharp$, with $\theta(e_Gp)=0$; this $\theta$ is the map $\delta$ of [lem-sfb-group-space-square-zero-difference-additive] for $T=H$, so it sends products in $K_B$ to sums. Put $\theta_f=\theta(f)$. Here $e_0=e_{S_0}\circ p_0$, where $e_{S_0}$ is the composite $S_0\to S\xrightarrow{e_G}G$ and $p_0:H_0\to S_0$; so $e_0^*\Omega^1_{G/S}=p_0^*E$ with $E=e_{S_0}^*\Omega^1_{G/S}$ on $S_0$, the cotangent module relative to $S$, not a substituted smooth model. By [lem-sfb-scheme-etale-relative-differentials-comparison] with $U=G$, $V=S$, the etale differential module of $G$, which represents $S$-derivations, is the associated etale module of the Zariski sheaf $\Omega^1_{G/S}$, and the latter is affine locally an associated module by [def-sc-relative-differential-sheaf], hence quasi-coherent. Its Zariski pullback $E$ is quasi-coherent by [lem-weil-pbc-module-pullback-quasi-coherent]. The equivalence [lem-trf-scheme-zariski-etale-quasi-coherent-equivalence], including its comparison with pullback, identifies these modules, $\widetilde{I[M]}$ and their homomorphisms on the Zariski and small etale sites. Thus we may use their ordinary quasi-coherent module descriptions in the next step. No finiteness of $E$ is required.

proof.text: Put $P=\Gamma(S_0,E)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-affine-tilde-gamma-adjunction], $E=\widetilde P$ and homomorphisms from associated modules are determined by their maps on global sections. Apply [lem-pc-flat-affine-base-change-sections] with $X=W=S_0$, coefficient ring $A_0$, extension $A_0\to B_0$, and module $E$. It identifies $\Gamma(H_0,p_0^*E)$ with $B_0\otimes_{A_0}P$, sending $b\otimes q$ to $b$ times the pullback of $q$. Since the pullback is quasi-coherent, the same adjunction identifies $\theta_f$ with a $B_0$-linear map $B_0\otimes_{A_0}P\to I[M]$. Equivalently it is an $A_0$-linear map $d:P\to I[M]$: the two inverse constructions are $q\mapsto\theta_f(1\otimes q)$ and $b\otimes q\mapsto b\,d(q)$. This uses only the tensor-product universal property, not an identification $\operatorname{Hom}(P,I)\otimes B_0=\operatorname{Hom}(P,I[M])$, which could fail for infinitely presented $P$. The identical construction on $H_0\times_{S_0}H_0$ has coefficient module $I[M\times M]$.

proof.text: The identity $f\circ m_H=(f\circ\operatorname{pr}_1)(f\circ\operatorname{pr}_2)$ is an equality of points of $G(C)$, each reducing to the identity in $G(C_0)$, so all three lie in the kernel $K_C$ of $G(C)\to G(C_0)$. Apply [lem-sfb-space-square-zero-lift-linearization] to the affine first order thickening $\operatorname{Spec}C_0\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}C$ with $a=e_Gp\circ\operatorname{pr}_1$; its coordinate on $K_C$ is the ring-sheaf difference $b^\sharp-a^\sharp$, a bijection onto its Hom module sending $a$ to $0$, and by [lem-sfb-group-space-square-zero-difference-additive] for $T=\operatorname{Spec}C$ it sends the product in $K_C$ to the sum. Under precomposition by any of $m_H,\operatorname{pr}_1,\operatorname{pr}_2$, the difference $f^\sharp-(e_Gp)^\sharp$ is postcomposed with the corresponding ring map: $h^\sharp\circ(f^\sharp-(e_Gp)^\sharp)$, since $(f\circ h)^\sharp=h^\sharp\circ f^\sharp$ and $e_Gp\circ h=e_Gp\circ\operatorname{pr}_1$. On the coefficient ideals these ring maps are exactly $\Delta_I,L_I,R_I:I[M]\to I[M\times M]$ from step 1. The tensor/sections identifications in step 3 send $1\otimes q$ to the pullback of the same section $q$ of $E$, so they commute with these maps, directly on pure tensors. Thus for every $q\in P$ the group identity gives\n$$\Delta_I(d(q))=L_I(d(q))+R_I(d(q)).$$\nThis proves the needed naturality explicitly, and uses the difference coordinate and its additivity for $C\to C_0$ as well as for $B\to B_0$.

proof.text: For fixed $q$, write $d(q)=\sum_m i_m e_m$ with finite support and $i_m\in I$. Step 4 is an equality in the direct sum $\bigoplus_{(u,v)\in M\times M}I e_{(u,v)}$. At $(m,m)$ for $m\ne0$ the left coefficient is $i_m$ and the right coefficient is zero, so $i_m=0$. At $(0,0)$ the equality is $i_0=i_0+i_0$, so additive cancellation gives $i_0=0$. Hence $d(q)=0$ for every $q$, whence $d=0$, $\theta_f=0$, and $f=e_Gp$ by steps 2 and 3. This is valid with torsion in $I$ or $M$, in characteristic $2$, and for the zero ring; it makes no inference from geometric points.

proof.text: For the original nilpotent $J$, let $A_r=A/J^r$ and let $f_r$ denote the base change of $f$ to $\operatorname{Spec}A_r$, for $1\le r\le N$. Coefficientwise reduction identifies the source with $D_{A_r}(M)$ and preserves the displayed group operations. We induct on $r$. The assertion for $r=1$ is the hypothesis. If $1\le r<N$ and $f_r$ is trivial, the ideal $I_r=J^r/J^{r+1}$ in $A_{r+1}$ has square zero, since $2r\ge r+1$. Its quotient is $A_r$, and reduction of $f_{r+1}$ is $f_r$. Apply the square-zero assertion proved in steps 1--5 to $A_{r+1}$, $I_r$, and the base-changed group scheme $G_{A_{r+1}}$. It proves $f_{r+1}$ trivial. At $r=N$ the equality $J^N=0$ identifies $A_N=A$ and $f_N=f$, proving the result. If $N=1$, the hypothesis itself is the result. Neither this induction nor the square-zero argument assumes smoothness, flatness, separatedness or finite presentation of $G$.
